questions.q: On what date did Jawaharlal Nehru move the Objectives Resolution in the Constituent Assembly, and what were the three key ideals it proclaimed for the future Constitution?
questions.a: The Objectives Resolution was moved on 13 December 1946. It proclaimed India as an Independent Sovereign Republic and guaranteed justice (social, economic, political), equality, and freedom to its citizens. A wrong answer (e.g., giving the date as 15 August 1947 or listing "secularism" as an ideal in the Resolution) reveals the student confuses the Resolution with the Preamble or Independence Day, and has not distinguished the Resolution's specific language from later constitutional provisions.

questions.q: Nehru explicitly avoided using the word "democratic" in the Objectives Resolution. What was his reasoning, and what did he mean by saying "we have given the content of democracy in this Resolution"?
questions.a: Nehru argued that "republic" inherently contains democracy, so adding "democratic" would be redundant. He meant the Resolution provided the substantive content of democracy — justice, equality, freedom, and economic democracy (socialism) — rather than just the label. A wrong answer (e.g., "Nehru opposed democracy" or "the word was omitted by mistake") shows the student misses Nehru's distinction between procedural labels and substantive goals, and fails to grasp his emphasis on economic democracy over formal democratic structures.

questions.q: In his speech, Nehru referred to the American, French, and Russian revolutions. Identify one specific lesson he drew from each, and explain why he insisted "we are not going just to copy".
questions.a: From the American Revolution: a Constitution can endure and build a great nation. From the French Revolution: persistence against oppression (Oath of the Tennis Court). From the Russian Revolution: a new type of state addressing economic justice. Nehru insisted on not copying because India's "temper" and conditions required creative adaptation — Western models had their own failures and needed to learn from experiments elsewhere. A wrong answer (e.g., "Nehru wanted to copy the Russian model") reveals the student overlooks Nehru's explicit rejection of mechanical borrowing and his call for a synthesis of liberal democracy and socialist economic justice suited to India.

questions.q: Somnath Lahiri (Communist) and Govind Ballabh Pant (Congress) both critiqued the Objectives Resolution but from different standpoints. Compare their core objections.
questions.a: Lahiri argued the Assembly was a British creation operating under British guns, so its resolutions were hollow until real sovereignty was seized; he urged immediate declaration of independence and fight against imperialism. Pant, while supporting the Resolution, warned that minority safeguards must not create "divided loyalty" — citizens must owe allegiance to the State, not communities, or democracy would be doomed. A wrong answer (e.g., "both opposed the Resolution") shows the student cannot differentiate between a radical critique of the Assembly's legitimacy (Lahiri) and a nationalist concern about national unity (Pant).

questions.q: N.G. Ranga redefined "minorities" in economic terms. Evaluate how this redefinition challenged the dominant understanding of minority rights in the Assembly and foreshadowed the Directive Principles.
questions.a: Ranga argued the real minorities were the poor, tribals, and peasants — not religious groups — because they were structurally exploited and could not exercise formal rights without material protection ("props and ladders"). This shifted the debate from political representation (separate electorates) to substantive socio-economic justice, directly anticipating the Directive Principles' focus on economic rights. A weak answer (e.g., "Ranga wanted reservations for the poor") misses the conceptual breakthrough: Ranga exposed the gap between legal rights and effective enjoyment, forcing the Assembly to confront economic democracy as a constitutional obligation.

questions.q: Construct a historical argument: "The Objectives Resolution was both a product of its tumultuous time and a deliberate attempt to transcend it." Support your argument with three specific pieces of evidence from the debates.
questions.a: A strong answer will cite: (1) Nehru's reference to Partition violence ("images of desolation") as the backdrop, yet the Resolution's universal ideals; (2) the omission of "democratic" to avoid redundancy while embedding economic democracy, showing awareness of contemporary ideological contests; (3) the immediate debates on separate electorates (Patel, Pant) and minority definitions (Ranga, Jaipal Singh) proving the Resolution triggered the very clashes it sought to resolve. A poor answer lists facts without linking them to the "product vs. transcendence" tension, or uses evidence from later chapters (e.g., language debates) not yet relevant.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Objectives Resolution, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on 13 December 1946 in the Constituent Assembly, was the ______ document that articulated the core philosophy and guiding principles of the Indian Constitution.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a member of the ______ Assembly in December 1946, surrounded by the trauma of Partition and the euphoria of impending freedom.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a member of the Constituent Assembly in December ______, surrounded by the trauma of Partition and the euphoria of impending freedom.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the historical context and content of the Objectives Resolution, analyze Nehru's references to past revolutions and his insistence on not mechanically copying Western models, and evaluate how the Resolution's ideals shaped subsequent debates on minority rights, federalism, and the Preamble.
